name: Fort Dearborn — officers' quarters

documented_range.note: THE RANGE IS THE FORT'S, NOT THIS BUILDING'S. No source reached dates any individual building inside Fort Dearborn. It opens with the rebuild of 1816 (Andreas; Wentworth quoting the Adjutant-General, 'the post was reoccupied about June, 1816 ... Nothing is on file respecting the rebuilding of the Fort') and closes with the demolition of the fort's principal structures in the summer of 1856 (Andreas). What carries the scene date is the middle: this building is drawn standing on the 1830 plan and described standing in Hubbard's 1827 walk round the inside, and the post was garrisoned continuously from June 1832 to 29 December 1836.

placement.position_note: READ OFF THE 1830 HARRISON PLAN. Position in pixels on the plate Andreas reproduces at vol. 1 p. 113, scaled at 1.10 ft per pixel (the scale derivation is on fort_dearborn_palisade and in docs/RESEARCH/fort_dearborn.md section 3), rotated to the sheet's true-north arrow, and hung on the fort centre at local E +1152, N +221. Carry +/-20 percent on the offset from the fort centre and +/-20 m on the fort itself. The facade bearing is the fort's 8-degree rotation plus the side of the parade this building faces, because every range in this fort fronts the parade. Hubbard, 1827: 'The old officers' quarters built of logs on the west, and within the pickets'. Andreas: 'The officers' quarters were on the west side'. The 1830 plan draws a long range against the west wall, and that range is this building.
placement.symbolic_location: Inside the west wall of Fort Dearborn, fronting east onto the parade.

footprint.note: TWO READINGS THAT DO NOT AGREE, AND THIS RECORD TAKES THE STATED ONE. The 1855 key gives 'the Officers' Quarters, B (wood, about 30x60 ft,)' - 9.14 x 18.29 m, which is the polygon here. The 1830 plan draws the west range about 30 ft deep and about 80 ft long at the scale this project derives, so the two agree on the depth to within 3 percent and disagree on the length by nearly 40 percent. THE STATED FIGURE WINS, and the reasoning is worth writing down because it decides several records: the scale that would overrule it was itself calibrated on the other stated figure in the same caption, so using it to correct that caption's second number is close to circular. What that costs is legible - the modelled building is about 6 m shorter than the plan draws its range - and it is why this footprint is inferred while the commandant's is documented. If the 1830 plan is right the officers were housed in an 80 ft range; if the 1855 caption is right they were in a 60 ft one; nothing reached settles it.

kind.note: Named as the officers' quarters by Hubbard in 1827, by Andreas's summary of the rebuilt fort, and by the 1855 photograph key.

construction.note: Hubbard, standing in the fort in 1827: 'The old officers' quarters built of logs on the west'. The 1855 key says 'wood', which is the same claim less precisely. A CORRECTION TO THIS PROJECT'S OWN DOSSIER: docs/research/04-structures-south.md section 1.2 reads Andreas as giving brick officers' quarters on the west and flags a conflict with the 1855 key. Andreas's page 84 states no material for them at all, and his page 264 - Hubbard's own words - says logs. The conflict was a misreading; the two sources agree.

stories.note: Not attested anywhere. Two is chosen because this range and the commandant's quarters are the two buildings the 1855 photograph shows as 'the principal buildings of the Fort', and a single-storey log range would not read as one of two principal buildings beside a two-storey brick one. That is an argument from a photograph nobody in this project has measured, so it is a guess and it is graded as one.

wall_height_m.note: No height is attested. 4.8 m is two storeys of log wall at period course counts. The number inherits the storey count's weakness above it.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal form for a log range of this period and plan.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested for any building in this fort. 34 degrees is the archetype's mid-range for a shingled or riven-shake roof of this period and span, and it is inferred from construction practice rather than measured.

chimneys.note: Not attested. A 60 ft officers' range through Chicago winters needs a stack at each end by type. The COUNT is the inference; position, size and material are the archetype's, per docs/LIBERTIES.md.

gallery.note: A NEGATIVE THAT IS ALSO A CHOICE. Captain Whistler's 1808 index to the FIRST fort says 'the Barracks are two storeys high with shingled Roofs and Galliaries fronting the parade' (Quaife), and galleries on the parade front are the type. Nothing says the 1816 fort's ranges had them, and John H. Kinzie says the two forts were 'differently constructed'. A plain front is rendered because nobody found evidence either way, which is itself a claim a visitor sees.

function.note: Quarters for the post's subordinate officers. In 1827, with the fort ungarrisoned, Hubbard found them occupied by Russel E. Heacock 'and one other American family' - which is evidence about 1827, not about 1835.

occupants.note: Not attested for 1835. Inferred from the building's function and from the post being garrisoned on the scene date; Hubbard's 1827 civilian tenants belong to the years when there were no troops.

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by John Baptist Baubian, 28 May 1835
land_owner.note: THE UNITED STATES RESERVATION. This is the same tract L108 already derives for `1835_no_build_ground.json` — from G1, Madison's line and the traced waterline — so the polygon is inherited rather than built again, and `check.sh` already re-derives it. The register's own row is the second, independent witness to the date L108 quotes from Andreas: Beaubien's pre-emption, 28 May 1835, five weeks before the scene date. The derived polygon is short of the documented 75.69 acres for the reasons L108 states, and is a floor rather than the reservation. WHETHER THE ENTRY HELD IS NOT READ HERE: it was disputed, and this row records the entry the register carries and nothing about its outcome. THE MARGIN IS ONLY 26 m, which is inside the working horizontal uncertainty of the georeference (about 20 m) doubled, so the grade drops a tier: the tract is right if the constructed line is, and nothing here proves the line to better than that. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

residents.name: The post surgeon's household
residents.why: A commissioned officer of the garrison lodged in the officers' quarters. The building is in the dataset and the practice is universal for a post of this kind; no source puts this man in this building, hence inferred.

persons.name: Dr Philip Maxwell
persons.note: A GARRISON OFFICER WHOSE TOUR BRACKETS THE SCENE DATE AT BOTH ENDS - 3 February 1833 to 29 December 1836 - which makes him one of the few people in the dataset whose presence on 1 July 1835 is a matter of record rather than of inference. Born at Guilford, Windham Co., Vt., 3 April 1799; practised at Sackett's Harbor, N.Y., and sat in the New York legislature before his appointment. He was a witness to the Indian treaty of 26 September 1833.

residents.research_note: THE ONE HOUSEHOLD IN THIS PARCEL WHOSE PRESENCE NEEDS NO ARGUMENT, and the one that identifies a missing building. Everything about Maxwell is dated: birth, appointment, arrival, treaty witness, departure. What is not in the dataset is the room he worked in. THE GARRISON IS UNDER-REPRESENTED HERE ON PURPOSE. Fort Dearborn on 1 July 1835 was an occupied post under Major John Greene with an enlisted company, and this parcel writes only the two officers the sources name and date. Every private soldier is a documented human being whom no source in this dataset names, and turning a muster strength into person records is derived-phase work with a muster roll, not something to guess at now.

what_it_supplies: the fort's plan arrangement: a quadrangular picket enclosure, corner works, four ranges, two gates
which building stood on which side of the parade
the relative proportions of the enclosure and the buildings in it
the fort's rotation relative to true north
the named ground around the fort: garrison garden, cultivated field, barn, wash house, well, shop, cemetery, ferry
what_it_does_not_supply: any dimension in feet - there is no scale bar
elevations, heights, roof forms or materials
the state of the fort in 1835 - it is five years earlier
a separation between the 1830 survey and the settler-memory additions the plate admits to

what_it_supplies: the commandant's quarters at about 25 x 50 ft, brick
the officers' quarters at about 30 x 60 ft, wood, at the north-west corner
which buildings stood on which side of the parade
the commandants of the second fort by date
the date the pickets came down is NOT given - only that it was 'at an earlier date' than 1850
what_it_does_not_supply: anything about the fort in 1835 that is not inferred backwards from an 1850 or 1855 image
a reliable division between first-fort and second-fort description - the pamphlet reprints both and readers routinely mix them

research_note: The west range. Its footprint note carries the one real dimensional disagreement in this complex and the reasoning that settled it; its construction note carries a correction to this project's own dossier, which had manufactured a brick-versus-wood conflict out of a page that says logs. See docs/RESEARCH/fort_dearborn.md sections 4 and 6.
